source: Friction on Ramps
Find the angle where a block starts to slip, tan θ = μ_s, and its acceleration once it slides.
Students point friction down the slope for a block that is sliding down.

Put together Inclined Planes and Static Friction, and a ramp becomes a friction meter. Tilt a board slowly with a block on it: at first static friction holds it, then at one particular angle it lets go.

A block starts to slip when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$. Once sliding down, kinetic friction points up the slope: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$. Sliding up, both gravity's part and friction point down the slope: the deceleration is $g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

Along the slope, gravity pulls with $mg\sin\theta$; static friction can resist with at most $\mu_s F_N = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$. The block holds while $mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, that is, while $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$. The mass cancels, so a heavy block and a light one of the same material slip at the same angle. Friction always opposes sliding (or the sliding that would happen), so its direction flips when the motion does.
With μ_s = 0.5 the block holds until tan θ = 0.5, at θ ≈ 26.6°; then it slides with kinetic friction.
Worked examples
A block sits on a board with $\mu_s = 0.6$. At what angle does it slip?
The slipping angle
about $31.0^\circ$
At the limit: $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\tan\theta = 0.6$.
$\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.6) \approx 31.0^\circ$.
A block slides down a $35^\circ$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.2$. Find its acceleration.
Sliding down
about $4.02\ \text{m/s}^2$
Friction points up the slope, against the sliding.
$$a = 9.8(\sin 35^\circ - 0.2\cos 35^\circ) = 9.8(0.574 - 0.164) \approx 4.02\ \text{m/s}^2$$ down the slope.
The same block is shoved up the same ramp. While it slides up, what is its deceleration?
Shoved up the slope
about $7.23\ \text{m/s}^2$
Now gravity's part and friction both point down the slope.
$$a = 9.8(0.574 + 0.164) \approx 7.23\ \text{m/s}^2,$$ so it stops quickly, then slides back down at $4.02\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Pointing friction down the slope for a block that is sliding down. Friction resists the sliding, so it points up the slope. Check: for a block sliding down, its acceleration must be smaller than the frictionless $g\sin\theta$; if your answer is bigger, friction has the wrong sign.
